name: The Nature Conservancy (charityevals)
summary: The Nature Conservancy (TNC), the largest conservation charity by spending, buys and protects land and water in the US and about 80 countries, brokers debt-for-nature deals with governments, and works on clean energy, food systems and fresh water. We model its fiscal year 2025 (July 2024 to June 2025, $1.28 billion of conservation spending including land purchases). The land it bought and its deal work (the year's Ecuador Amazon debt conversion and ocean plans) are modelled through forest carbon kept, local incomes and a small cut in pandemic risk. The other three-quarters of the spending (stewardship, restoration, fresh water, fisheries, adaptation, food systems and clean energy) publish no programme-wide outcome data, so they are valued at the result of the same kind of work on the site, discounted for missing data: Clean Air Task Force and three other energy-policy charities for clean energy; the Good Food Institute and the Coalition for Rainforest Nations for food systems; the Coalition for Rainforest Nations and the Woodland Trust for land policy, and the Woodland Trust alone for hands-on land and water management. The result is about 0.04 years of healthy life per $1,000, almost all of it from that comparison: the modelled deals and purchases add under 1%, because TNC is a small share of the resources behind its largest deal and kept forest carbon is worth little in healthy years. The biggest uncertainties are the unpublished split of spending, what the unmeasured programmes achieve, and the harm a tonne of CO₂ does.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Programmes with no outcome data
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for a programme that publishes no outcome data at all: it is valued at the result per dollar of the same kind of work elsewhere on the site, read live, and counts less by the shared slider "How much we count a programme we could only estimate from similar ones" (docs/normalization.md 2.12). A programme with some outcome data is modelled from it in the chain above, with wide ranges, never here.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Spending modelled in the chain: land and easement purchases plus the deal work, FY2025
rows.explainer: The two parts of TNC's conservation spending whose outcomes we can count from its reports: the year's land and easement purchases ($205.8 million) and its share of the conservation activities spent on brokering and supporting the Nature Bonds and Enduring Earth deals (deal_share). The rest of the activities is in proxy_program_spend (templates.md Conventions 1 and 12).

rows.label: Conservation activities and actions, FY2025 (year to 30 June 2025)

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Consolidated Financial Statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, report dated 19 December 2025)
source.page: Consolidated statement of activities, year ended June 30, 2025, p. 4

rows.explainer: The cash cost of TNC's conservation work in its fiscal year 2025 (July 2024 to June 2025), in thousands in the statement. It leaves out the book value of land TNC sold or gave away in the year ($113.6 million), which is land bought in earlier years: its cost is counted when it is bought (next row), not again when it is passed on.

rows.label: Purchases of conservation land and easements, FY2025

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Consolidated Financial Statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, report dated 19 December 2025)
source.page: Consolidated statements of cash flows, p. 8
source.quote: Purchases of conservation land and easements (205,790)

rows.explainer: Land and easements TNC bought in the year. They are capitalised, so they appear in the cash-flow statement rather than among expenses; TNC's own annual report counts them with its programme spending, as we do, since a donor's dollar pays for them.

rows.label: Share of conservation activities spent on the Nature Bonds and Enduring Earth deal work
rows.explainer: TNC publishes no split of its spending by programme: the audited statements give one programme line, and the annual report's financial summary none either. Its audited statements (Note 1) list nine pathways under three priorities; two of them, Nature Bonds and Enduring Earth, are the large government deals whose outcomes the chain below counts (the Ecuador Amazon debt conversion, the ocean deals of the year). Equal shares would give 2/9 (22%); these are small teams of finance, policy and science staff whose deals are paid for mostly by others, so our guess is 10% of the activities (4-20%). Land purchases are counted in full beside it; the other seven pathways' activities (90%) are valued in the proxy section. The year's deal work also prepares deals that close in later years and supports earlier ones; as a past average, the year's spending is set against the year's closed deals, with the next-dollar slider.

rows.label: Total spending: conservation programme, administration and fundraising, FY2025
rows.explainer: $1,693.5 million, TNC's own "Total Expenses & Purchases of Conservation Land & Easements" in its 2025 annual report: the same basis as the programme row, so the overhead multiplier spreads administration and fundraising (25% of the total) over all of it.

rows.label: General and administration, FY2025

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Consolidated Financial Statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, report dated 19 December 2025)

rows.explainer: Management costs in the same year, spread over the programmes in proportion to their cost.

rows.label: Fundraising and membership, FY2025

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Consolidated Financial Statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, report dated 19 December 2025)

rows.explainer: Fundraising costs in the same year, spread over the programmes in proportion to their cost.

rows.label: Conservation programme spending: activities plus land and easement purchases, FY2025
rows.explainer: TNC's own measure of its conservation spending, $1,276.1 million in its 2025 annual report ("Total Conservation Program Expenses & Purchases of Conservation Land & Easements"): the activities plus the land bought, without the book value of land passed on.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programmes in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do: total spending ÷ conservation programme spending, both counting land purchases.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled program, including overhead
rows.explainer: The protection and restoration programme's cost in FY2025 with its share of administration and fundraising.

rows.label: Hectares newly protected in FY2025 (new-protection equivalents)
rows.explainer: The year's new protections from the two modelled parts: the Ecuadorian Amazon deal and the land and easements bought. Stewardship of the preserves TNC already owns, restoration, fire and forest management and freshwater work publish no hectare counts; their spending is in the proxy section, valued at land and forest peers.

rows.label: Ecuadorian Amazon: hectares of new protection the year's deal finances

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Ecuador announces debt conversion for Amazon conservation (15 December 2024)
source.quote: protect an additional 1.8 million hectares of forests and wetlands

rows.explainer: TNC's largest land deal of the year: Ecuador's debt conversion for the Amazon Biocorridor Program, closed in December 2024 (FY2025) with TNC's Nature Bonds Program, finances new protection of 1.8 million hectares of forests and wetlands over 17 years. Other big deals fall outside the year: Eternal Mongolia was signed in April 2024 (FY2024) and the Cochamó purchase in Chile closed in December 2025 (FY2026). The year's ocean deals (The Bahamas, 6.8 million hectares of marine protected areas, November 2024; the Seychelles marine spatial plan signed into law in 2025) store no counted carbon and enter through the livelihoods branch.

rows.label: Ecuadorian Amazon: hectares of existing protected areas whose management the deal improves

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Ecuador announces debt conversion for Amazon conservation (15 December 2024)
source.quote: improve the management of 4.6 million hectares of existing protected areas

rows.explainer: Existing protected areas the same programme funds better management of (rangers, plans, community agreements).

rows.label: Effect of better management of an existing protected area, relative to new protection
rows.explainer: A hectare already protected on paper loses less forest than an unprotected one, so funding its management prevents less loss than a new protection. Our guess is a quarter of a new protection's effect (10-50%), anchored on the protected-area effect below (deforestation 41% lower in protected areas): if unfunded paper parks deliver about half of a funded park's effect, better management adds the other half of a smaller remaining gap.

rows.label: Ecuadorian Amazon: hectares counted, in new-protection equivalents
rows.explainer: New protections plus improved management at its relative effect.

rows.label: Average price TNC pays per hectare of land or easement
rows.explainer: TNC doesn't publish the hectares it bought in the year, only what it paid. Our guess at the average price, $5,000 a hectare ($2,000-15,000), is anchored on US rural land values (USDA's 2024 Land Values survey puts pasture at about $1,800 an acre, about $4,400 a hectare, and cropland near $5,500 an acre); easements cost less than fee purchases, land near cities and coasts much more.

rows.label: Hectares of land and easements bought in the year
rows.explainer: The year's purchases at the average price: about 40,000 hectares at the best guesses.

rows.label: Years a protection counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer for a won deal or reform (normalization.md 2.9): the years TNC's deal brought the protection forward, not how long it lasts. A deal TNC didn't broker might have come later through someone else, and land it didn't buy might have been bought by another trust, so we count the shared years rather than the deal's 17 years of funding or a perpetual easement (and keep the counterfactual adjustment at 1, Convention 5).

rows.label: Years of protection, discounted
rows.explainer: Every year of protection, and the wait before it, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Climate: tonnes of CO₂ a year a protected hectare keeps out of the air (average over the year's hectares)
rows.explainer: Avoided emissions: each part's baseline loss rate × the share the protection prevents × the CO₂ a lost hectare releases, averaged over the hectares counted. About 0.4 tonnes a hectare a year. Leakage (clearing pushed elsewhere) isn't netted here; it is a negative share in unmodelled_benefits_adj. No carbon is counted for the ocean deals.
rows.formula: (amazon_ha * amazon_loss_rate * protection_effect * amazon_tco2_per_ha_lost + acquired_ha * acquired_loss_rate * acquired_protection_effect * acquired_tco2_per_ha_lost) / hectares_protected

rows.label: Forest lost in the Ecuadorian Amazon in 2022

source.title: MAAP #200: State of the Amazon in 2023 (Amazon Conservation)
source.quote: deforestation in the Ecuadorian Amazon was the highest on record in 2022 (18,902 hectares), up a striking 80% since 2021

rows.explainer: Primary forest lost in the Ecuadorian Amazon in its worst recorded year; averaged with 2021 below, so the baseline is a run-rate (Convention 9).

rows.label: Rise in Ecuadorian Amazon forest loss from 2021 to 2022

source.title: MAAP #200: State of the Amazon in 2023 (Amazon Conservation)
source.quote: deforestation in the Ecuadorian Amazon was the highest on record in 2022 (18,902 hectares), up a striking 80% since 2021

rows.explainer: With the 2022 figure, gives 2021's loss (about 10,500 hectares), so the rate below is the two years' average rather than the record year.

rows.label: Forest in the Ecuadorian Amazon

source.title: Timber Trade Portal, Ecuador: country context (FAO 2015)
source.quote: The majority of forests - approximately 9.9 million ha (nearly 80%) - is in the Amazon region.

rows.explainer: FAO's 2015 figure; MapBiomas's later count implies about 7.5 million hectares, the low end.

rows.label: Loss rate in the Biocorridor's lands relative to the Ecuadorian Amazon's average
rows.explainer: The Biocorridor covers both remote forest (lower pressure than average) and corridors chosen because they are threatened (higher). We take the regional average (1), with a range from half to twice it.

rows.label: Ecuadorian Amazon: yearly forest loss rate without the protection (2021-2022 average)
rows.explainer: The average of 2021 and 2022 losses over the forest area: about 0.15% a year at the best guesses. The record year alone (0.19%) is within site_vs_regional_loss's range.

rows.label: Share of the forest loss a protected area prevents

source.title: ScienceDaily (Oregon State University), Formal protected area designation reduces the rate of deforestation but does not prevent it; Wolf et al. (2021), Nature Ecology & Evolution
source.quote: They found protected areas' deforestation rate is 41% lower than that of unprotected areas.

rows.explainer: From a matched comparison of more than 18,000 protected-area parcels (Wolf et al. 2021, Nature Ecology & Evolution, doi 10.1038/s41559-021-01389-0) with similar unprotected land (elevation, slope, nearness to people). Protection slows forest loss but doesn't stop it. The range is ours (20-60%), for the spread between regions and between strict and multiple-use areas. This is the counterfactual for the forest itself; whether the protection would have come anyway is the years-a-win-counts slider (years_protected).

rows.label: Tropical primary forest lost worldwide in 2023

source.title: World Resources Institute, Global Forest Review: How much forest was lost in 2023?
source.quote: Total tropical primary forest loss in 2023 totaled 3.7 million hectares

rows.explainer: With the next row, the CO₂ released per hectare of tropical primary forest lost; also the denominator of the catastrophic-risk branch.

rows.label: CO₂ released by that loss

source.title: World Resources Institute, Global Forest Review: How much forest was lost in 2023?
source.quote: All this forest loss produced 2.4 gigatonnes (Gt) of carbon dioxide emissions in 2023

rows.explainer: Gross emissions from the year's tropical primary forest loss.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂ released per hectare of tropical primary forest lost
rows.explainer: About 650 tonnes a hectare: the tropics' average, which fits a lowland Amazon forest.

rows.label: Land bought: yearly conversion rate without TNC's purchase
rows.explainer: TNC buys land under threat of development, logging or farming, mostly in the US. Our guess, 0.4% a year (0.1-1.5%), is a few times the US average loss of natural land to development (about 0.1-0.2% a year in the USDA's National Resources Inventory), for parcels chosen because they are at risk. Small next to the Amazon branch either way.

rows.label: Land bought: share of that conversion ownership or an easement prevents
rows.explainer: Owning the land, or an easement on it in perpetuity, stops development almost entirely; we leave 10% for later sales, swaps and weak enforcement (range 70-100%).

rows.label: Land bought: tonnes of CO₂ released per hectare converted
rows.explainer: A mix of temperate forest (several hundred tonnes of CO₂ in trees and soil, not all of it released on conversion), grassland and wetland (tens of tonnes, mostly soil carbon): 150 tonnes a hectare (30-400).

rows.label: Hectares of forest and natural land kept from loss each year of protection
rows.formula: amazon_ha * amazon_loss_rate * protection_effect + acquired_ha * acquired_loss_rate * acquired_protection_effect
rows.explainer: Baseline loss times the share the protection prevents, for both parts: about 2,400 hectares a year at the best guesses.

rows.label: Tropical forest kept from loss each year of protection (Ecuador)
rows.explainer: The Amazon part of the row above: the tropical forest the pandemic-risk branch compares with the world's tropical forest loss.

rows.label: Climate: years until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The Ecuador programme declares its new protections and builds management over its first years (it is funded over 17), so the benefits start on average about three years after the year's spending (1-8). Discounted at the shared rate, as are the other branches' benefits.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: 0: forest and land carbon carries no fossil-fuel smoke, so no air-pollution deaths come with these tonnes (the climate skeleton's row, docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of this fuel, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: Not used: fuel_share is 0, so the smoke factor of a fuel doesn't apply to land carbon.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tonnes' bridge, as by the tco2e unit's conversion.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly (none here)
rows.explainer: Deaths a source counts directly beside the tonnes; 0 when the smoke is in air_pollution_weight, so nothing is counted twice.

rows.label: Health: people whose air, water, food or disease exposure the protection changes
rows.explainer: 0: the year's deals publish no health evidence (water quality, fire smoke, malaria) for the people around them. TNC's urban-tree trial in Louisville (Green Heart) is outside this programme and has no cost or reach to scale. Zoonotic disease is the catastrophic-risk branch.

rows.label: Health: DALYs averted per person per year
rows.explainer: Not used: no people are counted in the health branch (above).

rows.label: Livelihoods: people whose income or food security the protection changes
rows.explainer: People whose incomes the year's deals change: Indigenous and other communities in and around the Ecuadorian Biocorridor (a share of the Ecuadorian Amazon's roughly one million people) and fishers in The Bahamas and Seychelles, whose marine plans set fishing rules and no-take zones. TNC publishes no count; our guess is 150,000 people (30,000-600,000).

rows.label: Livelihoods: ln(consumption) gain per person per year
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on the largest matched study, Naidoo et al. (2019, Science Advances, doi 10.1126/sciadv.aav3006: more than 60,000 households near or far from 600 protected areas in 34 countries): households near protected areas with tourism had a 17% higher wealth index and were 16% less likely to be poor, with no evidence of harm on average, though protection sometimes cuts people off from land and fish. A wealth index isn't consumption, the Biocorridor and the marine plans bring little tourism, and gains build slowly, so our best guess is a small gain, 0.5% of consumption a year (ln 0.005), with a range from a 2% loss to a 4% gain.

rows.label: Wellbeing: people who visit or live with the protected nature
rows.explainer: 0 at the best guess: visitors to the newly bought land mostly would have gone to other nature nearby, and the Amazon and ocean areas get few visitors. The range allows up to 50,000 people a year whose life satisfaction gains.

rows.label: Wellbeing: life satisfaction gained per person per year (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Life-satisfaction points (0-10) a year for someone who gains access to nature: studies of green space find small effects (hundredths of a point); only reached at the range's high end, since nature_people is 0 at its best guess.

rows.label: Wild animals: animal-years whose welfare the protection changes
rows.explainer: 0: TNC claims effects on species and habitats, not on wild animals' welfare, and more animals living is not by itself a gain (the sign of a protected forest's effect on wild animals' welfare is unknown).

rows.label: Wild animals: days of disabling pain spared per animal-year (negative if more)
rows.explainer: Not reached (wild_animal_years is 0). On Ambitious Impact's pain scale the sign is unknown for a protected forest, hence the range across 0.

rows.label: Wild animals: days of pain spared (before adjustments)
Wild animals: chicken-equivalent pain days
rows.explainer: The species step (docs/normalization.md 2.4) with Rethink Priorities' welfare range; 0 here, since no wild animals are counted.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: deaths in a COVID-scale pandemic
rows.explainer: The shared figure: WHO's 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-2021, the pandemic the yearly chance above is defined by.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: fall in the yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic, per year of protection
rows.explainer: The year's avoided tropical forest loss (Ecuador only; the land bought is mostly temperate) as a share of the world's tropical primary forest loss × the share of pandemic risk that scales with it × the yearly chance: about 2 in a million a year, at the best guesses, before the adjustments. Assumes risk falls in proportion to forest kept, which no study has measured.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: yearly chance of a pandemic as deadly as COVID-19
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Marani et al. 2021): about 2% a year.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of new diseases whose emergence land-use change drives
rows.explainer: The shared figure (IPBES 2020): more than 30% of new diseases since 1960.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of the land-use risk that scales with tropical forest loss
rows.explainer: IPBES's land-use change includes farming expansion, settlement and wildlife trade as well as clearing tropical forest. We take half of the land-use risk as scaling with tropical forest loss, in proportion to the hectares lost (10-100%); Dobson et al. (Science, 2020) argue for cutting deforestation as pandemic prevention but give no dose-response. The least grounded number in the model.

rows.label: Share of the catastrophe's deaths that are of children under five
rows.explainer: COVID-19's excess deaths were mostly of older people and few of young children; a different pathogen could hit children harder (the range's top). Anchored on WHO's excess-mortality age profile (Msemburi et al. 2023, Nature: most excess deaths over 60).

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: School-age children were the least affected group in COVID-19; up to 5% for a pathogen like the 1918 influenza.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: About 15% of COVID-19's adult excess deaths were under 50 (WHO's age profile, most deaths over 60); up to 40% for a pathogen that kills young adults (1918 influenza). The rest are valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: A catastrophe's deaths are valued like every death on the site, by age band × your value of a life; no premium for their number. Future generations are the next two rows.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take
rows.explainer: 0: the world recovers from a COVID-scale pandemic; its deaths are counted above. The tiny high end allows for lasting damage.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: future years of healthy life kept, discounted
rows.explainer: Every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take (the long-run world population × the share lost), discounted for ever at the shared rate: the yearly loss ÷ $discount_rate. How much future generations count is your discount rate.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: How far to trust the effect figures here: the 41% protected-area effect is a global average from matched (not randomised) comparisons and may not hold for the Biocorridor's mix of new and existing areas (×0.9); the CO₂ per hectare is the tropics' average and the loss rate a two-year regional average, not the Biocorridor's own (×0.9). Together 0.8 (0.5-1), in line with the evidence discounts on land-carbon estimates in Founders Pledge's forest work on the site (coalition-for-rainforest-nations-founders-pledge).

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: both counterfactual questions are answered elsewhere, so they aren't asked twice (Convention 5). Forest that would have stood anyway is out of the avoided-loss rows (protection_effect: only 41% of the baseline loss is prevented), and a deal or purchase that would have come anyway through someone else is the shared years a win counts (years_protected).

rows.label: TNC's share of the resources behind the outcomes (weighted by avoided CO₂)
rows.explainer: The two parts' shares weighted by the CO₂ each avoids, applied to every branch: about 6%, close to the Ecuador deal's share since it avoids almost all the CO₂. The livelihood and pandemic-risk branches also come mostly from the Ecuador and ocean deals, where TNC's share is similarly small. The ocean deals' livelihoods take the same share: TNC structured them the same way (Nature Bonds debt conversions paid for by the governments' savings), so the Ecuador share stands in for them.
rows.formula: (amazon_ha * amazon_loss_rate * protection_effect * amazon_tco2_per_ha_lost * amazon_attribution_share + acquired_ha * acquired_loss_rate * acquired_protection_effect * acquired_tco2_per_ha_lost * acquired_attribution_share) / (amazon_ha * amazon_loss_rate * protection_effect * amazon_tco2_per_ha_lost + acquired_ha * acquired_loss_rate * acquired_protection_effect * acquired_tco2_per_ha_lost)

rows.label: Ecuador deal: TNC's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: The Biocorridor is paid for by about $460 million over 17 years from Ecuador's debt savings, made possible by an IDB guarantee, DFC political-risk insurance and Bank of America's financing, with Indigenous nations co-designing and the government delivering. TNC designed the deal and gives technical support; its own cost isn't published but is likely in the tens of millions over the years of preparation and support. Its share of all resources is about 5% (2-15%). This is TNC's share of the deal's own resources over its life, not of TNC's yearly deal budget (that is in the cost).

rows.label: Proceeds from sales of conservation land and easements, FY2025

source.title: The Nature Conservancy, Consolidated Financial Statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, report dated 19 December 2025)
source.page: Consolidated statements of cash flows, p. 8
source.quote: Proceeds from sale of conservation land and easements 91,545

rows.explainer: TNC sells much of the land it buys to government agencies and other conservation owners, who pay part of the cost.

rows.label: Land bought: TNC's share of the money behind it
rows.explainer: Agencies and other buyers pay back part of what TNC spends on land: FY2025's sales proceeds over its purchases, a steady-state ratio (the land sold in a year was mostly bought earlier). About 56% is TNC's own.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: The two parts' delivery weighted by the CO₂ each avoids: the Ecuador deal at amazon_implementation_adj, the land bought at 1 (delivered at purchase). Applied to every branch, which come mostly from the deals. The ocean deals' livelihoods take the same delivery share, as government-run programmes of the same kind.
rows.formula: (amazon_ha * amazon_loss_rate * protection_effect * amazon_tco2_per_ha_lost * amazon_implementation_adj + acquired_ha * acquired_loss_rate * acquired_protection_effect * acquired_tco2_per_ha_lost) / (amazon_ha * amazon_loss_rate * protection_effect * amazon_tco2_per_ha_lost + acquired_ha * acquired_loss_rate * acquired_protection_effect * acquired_tco2_per_ha_lost)

rows.label: Ecuador deal: share of the programme's targets delivered
rows.explainer: The share of the Biocorridor's targets (1.8 million hectares newly protected, 4.6 million better managed) we expect to be delivered over its years: such programmes often fall behind on declarations and enforcement. 70% (40-90%), anchored on Brazil's ARPA programme, the model for these deals, which met its area targets with uneven management.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1: the other money behind the deals (Ecuador's debt savings, guarantees, government buyers of land) is already counted in TNC's share above, so leverage isn't counted again; a donation to TNC doesn't obviously displace other funders. Range 0.85-1.1.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Effects of the deals and purchases not modelled, as a share of modelled value. Negative: leakage, forest clearing pushed onto unprotected land (studies of protected areas find from none to about 40% of the avoided loss displaced). Positive: the Biocorridor's 18,000 km of river protections, water regulation and flood protection, and the year's land gifts ($48.1 million of contributed land and easements, not counted in reach). Net −10% (−40% to +20%). TNC's other protection work is not here: it is in the proxy section with its own spending.

rows.label: Livelihoods and catastrophic risk, in GiveWell units of value (before adjustments)
rows.formula: livelihood_people * ln_gain_per_person_year * protection_years * $uov_per_ln_consumption + catastrophe_deaths * annual_risk_reduction * protection_years * catastrophe_value_per_death

rows.label: Livelihoods and catastrophic risk, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from UoV into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Wellbeing from nature, in wellbeing-adjusted life years (before adjustments)
Wellbeing from nature, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from WELLBYs into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Spending on programmes with no outcome data, FY2025: the other seven pathways
rows.explainer: The conservation activities outside the deal work (90% at the best guess): stewardship of TNC's preserves, restoration and natural climate solutions, transformative protection, fresh water, regenerative food and supply chains, fisheries, adaptation and the clean-energy transition. TNC reports goals and project stories for these but no outcome data for the programmes as a whole, so they are valued at comparable programmes' results, by kind.

rows.label: Of that spending, share on the clean-energy transition
rows.explainer: One of the seven unmodelled pathways (1/7 = 14%), as TNC's Note 1 lists them; no spending split is published. Range 8-25%.

rows.label: Of that spending, share on regenerative food and deforestation-free supply chains
rows.explainer: One of the seven unmodelled pathways (1/7 = 14%); range 8-25%. The other five (stewardship and restoration, transformative protection, fresh water, fisheries, adaptation) are land, water and ocean protection, valued at the land and forest peers.

rows.label: Of that spending, share on land, water and ocean protection, restoration, fisheries and adaptation
rows.explainer: The rest: five of the seven pathways.

rows.label: Of the land, water and ocean part, share that is policy and finance work (natural climate solutions, transformative protection)
rows.explainer: Two of the five land, water and ocean pathways (40%, range 20-60%) are policy and finance work for protection and natural climate solutions, the kind the Coalition for Rainforest Nations does; the other three (fresh water, fisheries, adaptation) are hands-on management of land and water, the kind the Woodland Trust does.

rows.label: Result per dollar of comparable programmes on the site (units of value per dollar you give)
rows.explainer: Each unmodelled pathway at the median result of the same kind of work on the site, read live and weighted by its share of the spending. Clean energy (proxy_energy_weight): Clean Air Task Force, Industrious Labs, Evergreen Collaborative and Future Cleantech Architects: policy work on clean energy and emissions, like TNC's energy-transition and siting work. Evaluators' recommended charities, so the comparison flatters an average programme; the missing-data discount takes some of that back. Food and supply chains (proxy_food_weight): the Good Food Institute (changing what food is produced) and the Coalition for Rainforest Nations (policy against deforestation, the aim of TNC's deforestation-free supply chains such as Pará's cattle tracing): the two nearest kinds on the site. Land, water and ocean protection, restoration, fisheries and adaptation (proxy_land_weight): the Coalition for Rainforest Nations (forest protection through policy and finance) and the Woodland Trust (buying, planting and managing woods): the land and forest conservation models on the site, for TNC's stewardship, restoration, protection, freshwater, fisheries and adaptation work. Within the land part, the policy and finance pathways (proxy_land_policy_share) take the median of both; fresh water, fisheries and adaptation, hands-on management, take the Woodland Trust alone.
